utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: Good morning, Your Honours. Good morning to everyone in and around the courtroom. This is case IT-08-91-T, the Prosecutor versus Mico Stanisic and Stojan Zupljanin. Thank you, Your Honours.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HALL
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. Registrar. Good morning to everyone. First of all, I note for the record that we reconvene under Rule 15 bis; Judge Harhoff being and sent. May we have the appearances for the day, please.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: Good morning, Your Honours. Joanna Korner and Crispian Smith for the Prosecution.

utterances.speaker: MR. CVIJETIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Good morning, Your Honours. Representing Mr. Mico Stanisic's Defence, Mr. Slobodan Cvijetic and Ms. Eugene O'Sullivan.

utterances.speaker: MR. KRGOVIC
utterances.text: [Previous translation continues] ... good morning, Your Honours. Dragan Krgovic, Igor Pantelic, and Aleksandar Aleksic, and Jason Antley, our Case Manager, appearing for Zupljanin Defence.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HALL
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: Your Honours, I'm going to ask to go into private session in a moment to deal with the next witness's protective measures. But before I do that, you may recall that a couple of days ago I raised the question of outstanding matters, one of which was the Mladic notebooks and a ruling. Your Honours, in the last few days, I've been going through the witness who is going to be the first witness after Your Honours' -- after the break, in other words, on Monday week, and the Mladic diaries are relevant to him. And we give no method at the moment of uploading them into e-court, even, because we don't know whether they are going to be added to our 65 ter list. So, if at all possible, it would be very helpful if we could have the ruling this afternoon, given, as I say, the absence in the next week. Because, otherwise, we're going to start on Monday morning not knowing what the situation is, Monday week.

utterances.speaker: MR. PANTELIC
utterances.text: I do apologise, which witness you are mentioning, Ms. Korner?

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: [Microphone not activated] ... the one who's coming Monday week.

utterances.speaker: MR. PANTELIC
utterances.text: Yeah, but do we have a name just to have reference?

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: [Microphone not activated] ... ST -- the number of the witness I'm just -- asked for ... ST-215.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HALL
utterances.text: Yes, we will seek to have a decision on that by the end of today, Ms. Korner. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: Thank you very much, Your Honours. Your Honours, can I ask that we go into private session.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HALL
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: And we're back in open session, Your Honours.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HALL
utterances.text: Thank you. Is it the expectation of counsel that we reconvene for a third session to dispose of this exhumation matter?

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HALL
utterances.text: Any idea how long you -- you expect to be?

utterances.speaker: MR. ZECEVIC
utterances.text: Your Honours, it's very hard for me to say, but I guess my submission is half an hour, 45 minutes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HALL
utterances.text: Very well. So we'd would resume in 20 minutes.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZECEVIC
utterances.text: Your Honours, with your leave, I have two preliminary matters before we start with the exhumations submissions. First of all, Your Honours, I would like to inform the Trial Chamber that 1D370, MFI document, pending -- it was MFI'd pending translation. The translation was uploaded, and I would kindly ask -- move the Trial Chamber to remove the MFI of the document. 1D370.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HALL
utterances.text: Yes, so ordered.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZECEVIC
utterances.text: Thank you very much. Your Honours, I believe we should go into private session because it refers to a confidential document and I wouldn't like to make any mistakes about it.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HALL
utterances.text: Yes, we go into private session.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: We're back in open session, Your Honours.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: Your Honour, can I just very quickly explain the basis of this legal argument. Your Honours will recall that on the 23rd of July of this year we filed a motion to add the proof of death database to our 65 ter exhibit list and tender it into evidence and also asked to remove earlier versions of that. Your Honours, the database which has been put together by, in fact, a number of different analysts, because it began way back in 2001, I believe, contains the evidence showing the -- how the Prosecution are able to arrive at the lists which are attached to the schedules of the indictment of people who died in the scheduled incidents of this indictment.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HALL
utterances.text: [Microphone not activated] ... may I have a moment, please, Ms. Korner.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HALL
utterances.text: Ms. Korner, it occurs to us that, having regard to, without more, the nature of this evidence, that it may be more useful for the Trial Chamber to hear from the Defence first as to what their objection is.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: Yes, a --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HALL
utterances.text: Do you have a --

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: Your Honours, I thought I better just outline to you the basis of this objection before the Defence go into it, and that's this: In that database, there are extra names not mentioned in the schedules because since the schedules to the indictment were drafted, the examination by the analyst has shown that some extra, in fact, in all 1.700 names, can be shown to have died in these incidents - not new incidents; same incidents - that are listed on the indictment. But in each case or in most cases, Your Honours will see attached to the names of the -- that are listed in the indictment, the victims including other persons whose identities at this time are either not known or cannot be confirmed by the Prosecution. Where we've been able to establish further identities, that's in the database. That's the objection.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HALL
utterances.text: Thank you. Yes, Mr. Zecevic.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZECEVIC
utterances.text: Your Honours, I will speak in Serbian in order to be understood completely clear, and I have provided my submission to the interpreters for their benefit. [Interpretation] Your Honours, the procedural facts related to this issue are as follows: The document was first presented with this document, the exhumation spreadsheet, for the first time on the 22nd of July this year. At that point, we had talks with the OTP, suggesting that the Defence should inspect and analyse the document and inform the OTP about our position. Nevertheless, to your great surprise, the very next day, the 23rd of July, the OTP submitted to the Trial Chamber the motion proposing that this database be admitted. The OTP and the Defence held two meetings about this issue about which you have been duly informed. Which established, as Ms. Korner stated, that there was a preliminary, legal issue that had to be tackled with Trial Chamber's assistance before we could continue our talks about this problem. The problem is as follows, Your Honours: The second amended indictment in this case was filed on 10th of September, 2009, containing Schedules A through G and an annex containing the list of identified victims in Schedules A and B. The list has a break down based on municipalities and incidents and contains 1.443 persons, with the exception of three cases: Firstly, the Bijeljina incident; secondly the TO warehouse in Donji Vakuf; and thirdly, the Bileca SUP. All the other listed incidents first give a list of victims. And then there is the following sentence, uttered by Ms. Korner: [In English] "Victims included other persons whose identities at this time are either not known or cannot be confirmed by the Prosecution." [Interpretation] I will continue in Serbian. In addition to this, there are two paragraphs of the schedule, item 9.4, the firstly claims two unidentified men as victims. And then item 14.4, it reads, about 150 persons whose identity is unknown to the Prosecution or cannot be verified by the Prosecution at this point in time. Your Honours, may I remained you that it was on several different occasions during the pre-trial stage that the Defence pointed out the absence of clear facts in the indictment. We demanded that additional facts be provided. Our motion was thrown out by the Trial Chamber on two separate occasions, in 2005 and 2009. Having received the database, the exhumation spreadsheet, on the 22nd of July, the Defence concluded that the database had contained as many as 1.795 persons whose names are not to be found in any of the annexes to the indictment. I have to say what our position is. We find it difficult to accept that during the entire investigation, as Ms. Korner suggested, between 2009 -- 2001 and 2009, when the indictment was eventually raised and published, there had been a total of 1.443 persons listed in the annexes. What happens a mere year later on, after the beginning of trial, and no less than 18 years after those persons allegedly went missing or were killed, we have an additional 1.795 victims. Your Honours, the fact remains that when we analysed this documentation which runs into over 1.000 pages and is therefore quite comprehensive. The database contains 80 persons whose date of death falls outside of the scope of the time-period relevant to the indictment, which is 1992. We don't even have a date of death in the case of 582 persons. As for a total of 862 persons, their whereabouts are stated as "unknown." All I'm trying to do is give you some of the statistics that we found upon inspection, and I'm using these pieces of information by the way of an illustration. Believe me, there is more. For this reason, from the Defence's point of view, this is a complex problem. On the one hand, one is trying to add a total of nearly 2.000 new victims. On the other hand, the inadequacy of the information contained in the database, combined, at least in our submissions, these facts no doubt constitute a violation of the Tribunal's Statute, specifically Articles 21 and 20, and stand in the way of the fair trial that our clients are guaranteed by that very Statute. May I, please, first consider the addition of 1.725 new victims. The Prosecutor claims that they have the right to amplify the victim list during the actual trial and make this addition of 1.795 new persons a theory, which the Defence would like to challenge. For that purpose, we would like to put forward the following arguments. Your Honours, each new victim is a new allegation of crime. In this sense, it is a material fact that must be stated in the indictment in a timely manner with sufficient detail provided. There was no preliminary announcement to the effect that the Prosecutor was intending to amplify or add to the indictment by introducing new victims. In an annex to the indictment, we find some remarks next to each and every one of the incidents. In our view, these remarks do not as such make clear the intention of the Prosecutor to add new victims in this sense. If that is true, Your Honours, then we are at a loss as to how to explain items 9.4 and 14.4 in the annex. The only way to explain these or to interpret these is as some form of notice, an announcement by the OTP that new victims would be identified in that portion. If indeed the OTP get hold of such information at any stage during the proceedings. This amplification or extension of the witness list was never announced. We were not given notice of that. It is quite logical that the Defence has not been able to mount any sort of investigation or prepare itself until such time as a document was disclosed to us on the 22nd of July this year. Hence, we believe that in this case the Prosecutor has not proceeded with due diligence. They had this information long before the information was disclosed to us. The simple reason being this database is kept by the OTP. It is in their possession. Our learned friends have access to it on a daily basis, access to the database itself, as well as any information concerning potential new victims. In our submission, amending an indictment in this way at such a late stage in the proceedings leaves the Defence at a distinct disadvantage, simply because we have no time to verify these allegations. In order to do that, we would have to cease all other preparations for this trial and come to grips with that. Any information available to us right now cannot be verified. For example, by interviewing witnesses who have already appeared. I will briefly quote some jurisprudence before this Tribunal regarding this problem. I'm trying to make sure no errors occur. Therefore, I'll be quoting in English. [In English] [Previous translation continues] ... Prosecutor versus Krnojelac decision on preliminary motion on form of indictment -- amended indictment 11 February 2000, paragraph 54. "It is abundantly clear that the content of the schedules form an integral part of the indictment and that they have been added in that form in order to avoid cluttering up the text of the indictment at the places where they are so described. They must be treated as if they were incorporated into the text at those places. The general allegations of the individual and superior responsibilities of the accused made in paragraphs of the indictment apply to those schedules in the same way as they applied to any other part of the indictment." And, additionally, Kvocka appeals decision, paragraph 67: "In a recent case, the Appeals Chamber held that an indictment must necessarily, in the absence of special order, consistent of one document, that schedules to an indictment form an integral part of the indictment, and that -- that they can contain essential material facts omitted from the body of the indictment. In the case under appeal, the Appeals Chamber sees no reason to depart from this approach. The events contained in the schedules amount to material facts that have to be proven before the accused can be held responsible for the crimes contained in the indictment. The Trial Chamber, therefore, in this case, correctly reached this conclusion." [Interpretation] Your Honours, as for the Tribunal's jurisprudence, I have here a total of 12 documents, 12 Judgements. I have delivered this list to our friends from the OTP. I would not like to take up more time than necessary and quote each and everything single one; therefore, my proposal is to have this list distributed to officers of the court so that they can familiarise themselves with our position on that matter, regarding the Tribunal's jurisprudence. As for the other aspects. The inadequacy of the database. Your Honours, I will reflect upon that very briefly. Based on our analysis, which you will realize is quite a comprehensive one, of such documents as we received from the OTP, we have concluded that the documentation is not appropriate to form a basis for a Court ruling. The documentation manifests a number of shortcomings. The documents were not verified nor indeed were they cross-referenced based on a -- different sources. I think the best way to illustrate this to the Trial Chamber would to be use an example. I'm doing my best not violate any provisions regarding secrecy and confidentiality. I will name specific instances from the indictment, but the names and figures are purely fictitious. We have a situation where one of the witnesses states that five people were detained. His names are unknown to the witness. For example, on 20th of July these people were taken away from Omarska. They never returned. The suspicion is well-founded that these people are no longer alive. Based on such information, an entry was made to the OTP's database, hence we come across an allegation about five persons taken away from Omarska on 20th of July, 1992, who are listed as missing. Now we have another witness who says, On or around 20th of July Muhamed Muhamedovic [phoen] and his two sons and two other persons were taken out of Omarska and never returned. The names are fictitious. Now, this is again entered into the database. And then we have Muhamed Muhamedovic and his two sons, called Muhamedovic, and two unknown persons, and they are listed as missing. We have a third witness, then, who says, I saw in July, Muhamed, whose last name I don't know, being taken out of Omarska with his four relatives and he never returned. Now, this is again entered into the database as additional five missing persons. And then we get another witness saying, On the 22nd of July, I was taken out of my village in the municipality of Prijedor to a site and then five or six other persons were brought in. They fired on us. I survived, and the rest didn't. Now, this bit of information is, again, entered into the database, and based on all of this, one can get the impression that four times five people, 20 in total, were killed; whereas, in the actual fact we're talking about the same five people mentioned in the statement by the first witness, the witness who didn't know those people. I think that we now have a duplication of victims in various incidents. And for the purposes of a criminal trial, this renders the database unusable. The Prosecution will surely say that the number is irrelevant here, and, as a matter of principle, I tend to agree. But what I would like to illustrate is this: The database is unreliable, because these data will probably lead to the conclusion that some of the persons never really existed, the ones who are entered in the database, because names are entered differently. They were not killed at all; they live abroad, they moved out. We had cases of this nature in Srebrenica. And this has engendered a great deal of controversy regarding the acceptance of adjudicated facts before this Tribunal and has been widely reported in the media. We would like to give some sources that are used for this database which lack objectivity, in our submission. Let me give you some examples. One of the sources is the Sarajevo Household Survey. Then we have the Muslims Against Genocide 2002 list. The third is The Book Of Missing Persons, Prijedor. These are all sources that were used to create this database, and in our submission, they lack objectivity. And the same goes for some other sources that were used in the creation of this database. The Defence has -- is of a view that regardless of the complexity of proceedings before this Tribunal, all the cases before it have been and are criminal proceedings that deal with the commission of specific crimes. Principles of criminal law, of evidence and procedure, are more or less universally acknowledged and recognised in all jurisdictions regardless of whether we are talking about the adversarial or inquisitorial system or a combination of the two, such as we have here at this Tribunal, and any diverging from these rules constitutes in its very essence the negation of those rules and directly violates the principle of fair trial which is universally guaranteed right of each and every accused. So, to sum up, the Defence opposes to the addition of persons who are not listed in the schedules to the indictment for reasons that I listed at the beginning of my submission; and, secondly, in light of the unreliability of the database, the Defence has notified the Prosecution that it would demand from the Prosecution to disclose to the Defence the minimum necessary information that would enable the Defence to identify each and every person listed in the schedules to the indictment, in a way which will make it possible for the Defence to challenge the allegation that the victims listed there are in fact the -- have -- were in fact the victims of the crimes that the accused are charged with. And this is consistent with the jurisprudence before this Tribunal. The victim must be identified in such a way that the Defence is able to challenge the allegation that these were indeed victims of a crime that the accused is charged with. The Defence has already submitted to the Prosecution the minimal information that it requires, and once it has been received, we would like to present our position regarding each and every victim in the schedules to the indictment, and I would now like to acquaint you with the minimum information that we require. One, first name last name. Second, father's name. Third, personal identification number of the victim. Four, place and date of the murder or disappearance. Place where the remains of the victim were found. The forensic findings regarding the cause of death. And the judicial decision to declare a missing person as deceased. We understand that the Prosecution might perhaps not have all this information for each and every victim. That's why we included some other items, because item 6 might assist us with items 4 and 5, and so on. Your Honours, this is my submission. Thank you very much for your time.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HALL
utterances.text: [Previous translation continues] ... Mr. Zecevic. Yes, Mr. Pantelic.

utterances.speaker: MR. PANTELIC
utterances.text: Yes, Your Honour. Just very briefly, because Zupljanin Defence is completely along the lines that my learned friend Mr. Zecevic explained and we were participating in this mutual contacts and negotiation with the OTP. First of all, just a small correction to the transcript. On page, 64 line 4, instead of Bijeljina it should Biljani as a site of incident, to have a clear record. Your Honours, adopting all points explained by Mr. Zecevic, I would like to respectfully ask this Trial Chamber to direct Office of the Prosecutor to amend the indictment or to reduce this list of alleged victims. Why? In light of -- I will make a short digression, which -- which is related to my submission. In light of the findings in Judgement of Simic et al., Samac case, the -- the OTP theory of that case was that more than 17.000 non-Serbs were prosecuted -- persecuted, deported, expelled from the municipality of Samac. At the end of the day, beyond a reasonable doubt, only 16 persons out of 17.000 of non-Serbs were considered as a persons persecuted or deported. This illustration, Your Honours, gives me a right to respectively ask this Trial Chamber, in order to avoid this huge basis, crime bases where our friends from the OTP are comfortably swimming, and this ocean of concept of JCE category 3 is very warm and comfortable sea for them and that -- that's why they are doing what they are doing in this particular case. They are just adding and putting without any particular minimum requirements by the criminal case just the names. As illustration, in these Confidential Annexes, they even don't have a name, they have just abbreviation, like LNU, et cetera, or FNU, et cetera. I believe that, in quest for justice, this process might -- should go along the -- very precise rules and very precise categories. And that's why I think that the OTP should precisely enumerate victims with all necessary elements, and to, accordingly, amend the indictment or present this particular piece of evidence or case in support of their theory. Going into the thousands of names of alleged victims will inevitably bring us to the situation where we would not able to know for whom, how, when, and why certain criminal responsibility should arise. That's why I -- I support all -- all what -- all points what Mr. Zecevic outlined, and respectively ask this Trial Chamber to direct and to instruct Office of the Prosecutor to narrow this base and to help even Defence, to some extent, to -- to maybe find a solution with the Office of the Prosecutor of certain, maybe, undisputed facts or data, so that this trial could go smoothly -- as smoothly as possible. Thank you for your attention, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HALL
utterances.text: Yes, Ms. Korner.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: Your Honour, there are two wholly separate applications being made here. One of which is suitable for Your Honours' ruling, which is the first, whether we should be allowed to add the database containing the extra names; the second, the adequacy of the information in the database and/or on which the Prosecution rely is a matter of fact to be argued by evidence, if required. Can I make this quite clear: We have, from the beginning, told the Defence that we will at any stage supply them with the underlying information relating to the deaths which are in the schedules and in the database. Not -- not just recently but right from the beginning and, indeed, the question of the exhumation evidence has been raised from the pre-trial stage, as to how it was going to be dealt with. So if there is any suggestion that we have deliberately withheld that information, then we reject that. And as I'm sure Mr. Zecevic will agree, that has always been on offer. The second matter is this: The spreadsheets which the Defence have been provided with set out each and every piece of evidence, which is not just the Prijedor Book of the Dead or the -- whatever the other two documents that were quoted, but other evidence that goes with it, including statements, documents, and the like. And it's clear from the spreadsheet what the Prosecution offer. And, of course, the Defence can have those documents at any stage. It's a mammoth task but, of course, they are entitled to and we would never think of refusing it. Third on this point, which, as I say, is not a matter for Your Honours to rule on today, the Defence are entitled to challenge each and every name, the pieces of evidence which relate to those in the schedules of the indictment or in the database by insisting that the evidence is called. It's not being done in other case but that doesn't mean to say it can't be done. It is their right and we'll do it if they say so. It will take I don't know how many months to go -- to call every witness to explain how the person disappeared or died or he saw him shot, but we will do it. That is their right, subject to Your Honours' ruling on this matter. But as I say, that is not a matter on which Your Honours can rule. The Defence are entitled to put us to strict proof, and if that's what they do, then that is what we will do as well. On the matter of whether or not the extra names which are contained in the database should be admitted into evidence subject to the question of -- of proving each and every one of them, Your Honours, the -- the names, the averments in the schedules, whether those are material averments in the indictment depends on the proximity of the accused to the actual killings themselves. Tribunal jurisprudence has said that over and over again. Effectively, forget about the Simic case, which is a distinctly old case, but since the Brdjanin case onwards, when Judge Hunt made it clear in his ruling on the Brdjanin indictment, if I can just remind you of that and then remind Your Honours of the latest case, which is not on Mr. Zecevic's list, and this is at paragraph 18 of the objections -- the decision on the objections by Momir Talic, so Mr. Zecevic is probably familiar with it, to the form of the amended indictment, paragraph 18: "A distinction is drawn in the Tribunal's jurisprudence between the material facts upon which the Prosecution relies which must be pleaded and the evidence by which those material facts will be proved, which need not be pleaded. Whether a particular fact is a material one which must be pleaded depends, in turn, upon the nature of the case which the Prosecution seeks to make and of which the accused must be informed. The materiality of such details as the identity of the victim, the place and date of the events for which an accused is alleged to be responsible and the description of the events themselves necessarily depends upon the alleged proximity of that accused to those events." "In a case --" paragraph 19 -- "based upon superior responsibility --" which is what this case is -- "what is most material is the relationship between the accused and the others who s did the acts for which he is alleged to be responsible and the conduct of the accused by which he may be found to have known or had reason to know that the acts were about to be done or had been done by those others and to have failed to take the necessary and reasonable measures to prevent such acts or to punish. However so far as those acts of the other persons are concerned although the Prosecution remains under an obligation to give all the particulars which it is able to give, the relevant facts will usually be stated with less precision and that is because the details of those acts by whom and against whom they are done is often unknown and because the acts themselves often cannot be greatly in issue." Your Honours, in reality, that is the case here. The killings which are listed in the schedules to the indictment are not in fact, as far as we've been able to tell over the last year of trial, in issue. The question of the perpetrators may be, but not the acts themselves. In the recent decision in the Gotovina case, the original trial ruling on 9 October 2008 and the Appeals Chamber ruling in 2009 it was made absolutely clear that -- if I can get to the -- the right page: "The current Defence submissions --" this is paragraph 10 of the decision of 9th of October 2008 -- "The current Defence submissions also dealing with the lists on the indictment are derived from the supposition that the identities of victims constitute material facts which need to be pleaded in the indictment. The requirements of the pleading of the identities of victims have either, however, already been litigated before the Trial Chamber which, in its decision on Gotovina's preliminary motions, found that the Prosecution did not need to identify each and every victim in the indictment." However, Your Honours, I'm sorry there is one other case I think -- which I can't lay my hands on at the moment. What we've done here is where we have been able to identify them, and Your Honours, I think in the Popovic case that came up, which, at the moment, I can't lay my hands on, we are obliged to give that information to the Prosecution [sic]. And so what we've done here, Your Honours, it's not a question that all of this information is new information. It's the analysis of the information. Since the schedules were done, further analysis has been done of the information that was available, as a result of which, and as I say, it is all set out very clearly in the spreadsheet, we can identify, we submit, further names from each of the scheduled killings. This is not a new allegation. It is simply, if you like, giving further detail, for which the Defence in one sense should be grateful, of the names of those we say died at the -- at the various killings. And Your Honours we submit that in the end result, it may not make a huge difference. In fact, we very much doubt, given the nature of this case, in the event of a conviction, how many people, whether it was 1.700 or 3.000, died but there is an importance from the point of view of the record that those that the Prosecution can say are rightly listed as victims of these crimes should be listed. And so we say the addition of these names, leaving aside the proof, which is a totally separate matter, is one that properly should be admitted by this Trial Chamber. Your Honours, as Mr. Zecevic says, there are a number of authorities. We can provided also the list of the extra authorities. But the only issue, we say, that Your Honours can decide upon now is whether or not the database should be admitted into evidence containing those names.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HALL
utterances.text: Thank you. Well, we have your arguments and submissions on the record and we will give a ruling as soon as circumstances permit. Before we rise we do have a brief oral ruling to deliver. Judge Delvoie.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE DELVOIE
utterances.text: Yes, indeed. And it is an oral one because of the urgency of the decision in relation to the Prosecution's motion and further findings for the addition of the Mladic diaries to its Rule 65 ter list, the Chamber finds that of all the 22 diaries submitted, only the eight diaries from 1992 in their entirety and the five identified portions from 1993 but not the three related diaries may be added to the exhibit list. Further, the evidence of General Milovanovic will suffice in the view of this Chamber to establish the prima facie authenticity of the diaries, and therefore is added to the Prosecution's witness [sic] list in the interest of justice. Written reason of the decision will follow shortly.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: [Microphone not activated] is he -- the -- the -- can I -- just a moment.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: I think we need -- can we redact, please, the last part of Your Honours' ruling, from line -- page 78, line 15 to 18. Can we go into private session.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HALL
utterances.text: Yes, private session.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE DELVOIE
utterances.text: Just out of curiosity, Mrs. Korner, was your motion filed confidentially?

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: I can't remember, is the answer. I'm sorry, does that mean he is 92 bis? That's all I wanted to know, his evidence. In other words, his statement can go in. Because that's what we applied for.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE DELVOIE
utterances.text: No, Mrs. Korner, he will be viva voce. But you will read that in the written -- in the written reasons.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: Well, Your Honours, I would respectively ask that it be 92 ter. I don't want to have take him through every single -- or one of us take him through every single word he said in both the Stanisic, Simatovic, and Popovic and repeat it all. He can be there for cross-examination, and indeed I think the only objection to authenticity, which I may is utterly surprising given that it is not contested by either Karadzic or Perisic, however, is that the Defence can then cross-examine him if they really wish to pursue this line. But we would ask that it is 92 ter. Why on earth would we want to make him go through chapter and verse for the third time?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE DELVOIE
utterances.text: Let's see if -- if -- if you will uphold this application for 92 ter after having read the written reason, Ms. Korner.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: Certainly, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HALL
utterances.text: Thank you. And with that, we take the adjournment to Monday, the 27th of September, in Courtroom III, at 9.00 a.m. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HALL
utterances.text: to be reconvened on Monday, the 27th day of September, 2010, at 9.00 a.m. 25

procedural_notes.text: --- Whereupon the hearing adjourned at 1.49 p.m.,
